questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. Embedded and control systems
questions.question: A glass factory's security analyst, with no rights on the control network its engineers own, sees an unknown device sending commands to the furnace controllers as temperatures climb. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Block the device at the control firewall, then tell the engineers
options.B: Power off the furnace controllers from the server room
options.C: Actively scan the furnace network to find the device
options.D: Alert the control room operators and the control engineers

questions.key_concept: In OT, operators bring a running process to a safe state; security staff alert them and the system's engineers rather than act on the controls.
questions.pre_read: Think about what could happen on the factory floor in the next few minutes.
questions.correct_explanation: Climbing furnace temperatures can hurt people, and in operational technology human safety comes first. The control room operators can bring the furnace to a safe state by procedure, and the control engineers own the control network, so the analyst alerts both at once. Blocking the device is the runner-up because it targets the cause, but the analyst has no rights to change the control firewall, and a block does not cool an overheating furnace.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: blocking and telling the owners both matter. But the analyst has no rights on the control network, and a block does not make the overheating furnace safe.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because stopping the controllers seems to stop the danger. But cutting power to a running furnace's controls can itself be unsafe; operators make it safe by procedure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a scan would find the device fast. But active scans can freeze fragile controllers, adding risk to a process already in trouble.

tips: Eliminate: B cuts power to controls the operators need to make the furnace safe, and C actively scans controllers that such scans can freeze.
Final two: D beats A because the operators can make the furnace safe now and the engineers own the firewall change; blocking it yourself oversteps and leaves the heat climbing.
Exam cue: in OT, the operators who run the process bring it to a safe state. Security staff alert them and the system's engineers at once, then contain through the incident process.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 Section 2.4 (Comparing OT and IT System Security: human safety is paramount, followed by protection of the process); NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MA-04 (incidents are escalated or elevated as needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'with systems that move physical things, protect people first, then keep the process running' (notes 4.1.11 Embedded Systems and Industrial Control Systems). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up round 2 (31 Oct 2026): the stem says the control engineers own the control network, and A now also tells the engineers, so the key no longer stands out as the only owner-naming, two-party option.

questions.question: A gym chain's facilities manager owns its new door cameras, which all ship with the same default password; device hardening is the network technician's step in the setup procedure. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Give each camera its own unique password, then connect it
options.B: Connect them as shipped, relying on the edge firewall
options.C: Report the default passwords to the facilities manager
options.D: Keep the default but disable remote access on each camera

questions.key_concept: Default passwords are among the first things attackers try; when the setup procedure assigns the change, make it before the device connects.
questions.pre_read: Picture the first hour each camera spends on the network under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A shared default password is published and among the first things attackers try, so each camera needs its own before it connects. Device hardening is the technician's step in the setup procedure, so they set each camera's own password now. Reporting to the facilities manager is the runner-up because the manager owns the cameras, but the procedure gives this step to the technician, so reporting and waiting only leaves the published default in place longer.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the edge firewall blocks outside connections. But a compromised device inside can still reach the cameras, and default passwords are tried first.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the facilities manager owns the cameras and decides how they are used. But the procedure gives hardening to the technician, so reporting and waiting only delays the fix.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because closing remote access shuts one path in. But anyone on the inside network can still log in with the published default, so it must still be replaced.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the edge firewall to protect devices inside, and D leaves the published default in place for anyone already inside.
Final two: A beats C because the procedure gives this step to the technician; owners decide what falls outside the procedure, not the steps it assigns.
Exam cue: check the procedure before the org chart. A step it gives you is yours to do; the owner decides what it does not cover.

questions.question: A home builder's sales office runs staff computers, guest Wi-Fi and a payment terminal for deposits on one flat network. Which basis for dividing them into segments should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: By IP address order, filling each subnet in turn
options.B: By office floor, so each floor's devices share one segment
options.C: By trust level and purpose, so rules fit each group
options.D: By device type, so like devices share the same rules

questions.key_concept: Segments group systems that share a trust level and purpose, so rules between them can allow only the traffic each group needs.
questions.pre_read: Picture which devices would end up sharing a segment under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Segmentation works by putting systems with the same trust level and job together, then allowing only needed traffic between groups. Guests, staff computers and payment systems need very different protection, so they belong apart. Grouping by device type is the runner-up because similar devices often get similar settings, but a guest's laptop and a staff laptop are the same type with very different trust, so they would share a segment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because subnets are often filled this way. But address order says nothing about risk, and subnets without rules between them are not real segments.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because floors give a neat physical layout. But one floor mixes guests, staff and payment systems, so its segment would join devices needing very different protection.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: similar devices often need similar settings. But a guest's laptop and a staff laptop are the same type with very different trust, so they would share a segment.

tips: Eliminate: A groups by address order, which says nothing about risk, and B groups by floor, which puts guest and payment devices side by side.
Final two: C beats D because segment rules depend on trust and purpose; grouping by type would put a guest's laptop beside a staff laptop.
Exam cue: group by trust and purpose, then filter between the groups. Floor, address range or device type help only where they match trust.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7(21) (Boundary Protection | Isolation of System Components)

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Defense in depth
questions.question: A phone carrier's chatbot runs on a vendor's AI model with built-in content filters, and the product lead calls that enough. Which addition should the security analyst propose to BEST apply defense in depth?

options.A: Keep the vendor and model names out of public view
options.B: Upgrade to the vendor's stricter filters and log what they block
options.C: Add an edge firewall rule to block harmful chatbot replies
options.D: Check and log each chatbot reply before customers see it

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth adds a different kind of control at another point, such as checking replies before release; stricter vendor filters are still one layer.
questions.pre_read: Imagine someone tricks the vendor's filters with a clever prompt, and follow the reply.
questions.correct_explanation: Defense in depth needs layers that fail independently. The carrier's own reply check sits outside the vendor's model, so it can catch a bad reply the vendor's filters miss. NIST warns that checkers can share blind spots with the model, so the logs let staff spot misuse that gets past both. Upgrading to the vendor's stricter filters is the runner-up, but one trick may beat both, and their log shows only what they caught.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because secrecy can slow attackers a little. But anyone can still type tricky prompts into the chatbot, so hiding names cannot catch a harmful reply.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: stricter filters do improve that layer. But they are still the vendor's filters, so one trick could defeat both, and logging what they block shows nothing they miss.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because firewalls are a classic layer. But an edge firewall filters network traffic, not what a chatbot says inside allowed web sessions.

tips: Eliminate: C expects a network firewall rule to judge chatbot content, and A relies on secrecy, which cannot catch a harmful reply.
Final two: D beats B because the carrier's own check is a separate layer it controls; stricter vendor filters can be fooled the same way, and their log shows only what they caught.
Exam cue: a stronger version of the same control adds no depth; add a control of another kind at another point.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-8(1) (Security and Privacy Architectures | Defense in Depth); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.3.3 (Mitigations: output detection and activity monitoring add defense in depth, but detectors may fail together with the model they check)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'each layer should fail independently, and AI systems get layers too, including filtering and monitoring of outputs' (notes 4.2.5 Defense in Depth). Final pass (31 Oct 2026): A loses its reason clause and C is now a real (wrong-layer) addition; the explanation ties the NIST correlated-failure point to the logs and separates an added layer from limiting access. questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust components
questions.question: A record label is replacing its VPN with Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) for remote staff. Which difference should the network technician explain as MOST important?

options.A: Each verified user reaches only the specific apps they need
options.B: All traffic between staff and company systems becomes encrypted
options.C: Staff on company laptops no longer need to sign in
options.D: The office firewall and internal segments can be retired

questions.key_concept: A VPN places a user on the network; Zero Trust Network Access connects a verified user to specific applications, one session at a time.
questions.pre_read: Picture what a remote staff member can reach right after connecting, under each approach.
questions.correct_explanation: A VPN puts remote users on the internal network, where they can often reach far more than they need. ZTNA connects each verified user only to the applications they are allowed, one session at a time, and keeps checking. Encryption is the runner-up because ZTNA does encrypt traffic, but the VPN already did that, so encryption is not what changes.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: ZTNA does encrypt traffic in transit. But the VPN already did, so encryption is not the difference; the change is what each user can reach.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because company laptops are trusted assets. But Zero Trust grants nothing for owning a device or for its location; every user still signs in.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ZTNA moves checks to each application. But Zero Trust adds to firewalls and segmentation; it does not replace the network controls behind it.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts a device because the company owns it, and D assumes ZTNA replaces the firewall and segments behind it.
Final two: A beats B because VPNs and ZTNA both encrypt; what ZTNA changes is access to specific apps instead of the whole network.
Exam cue: a VPN connects you to a network; Zero Trust connects a verified user to a resource. Look for per-app, per-session access.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Zero Trust Network Access connects a verified user to one application and keeps checking; a VPN places the user on the network' (notes 4.2.7 Zero Trust Architecture Components). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): role changed to the canonical network technician (rule 11).

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Network access control
questions.question: At a convention center, a new digital sign cannot do the 802.1X sign-in that network access control (NAC) requires, and NAC exceptions need the policy owner's approval. What should the network technician do FIRST?

options.A: Admit the sign by its MAC address, which proves its identity
options.B: Refer the sign to the NAC policy owner for a decision
options.C: Turn off NAC on the sign's port, then tell the policy owner
options.D: Block the sign until it can do the 802.1X sign-in

questions.key_concept: Devices that cannot meet NAC get limited access through an exception the policy owner approves and records, never through a quiet bypass.
questions.pre_read: Picture the sign's network port tomorrow under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: The sign cannot use the normal NAC sign-in, so it needs an exception, and exceptions need the policy owner's approval. The technician sends the request; the owner can approve limited, profiled access that is recorded and time-limited. Turning off NAC first is the runner-up because the sign works sooner and the owner still hears of it, but it makes the owner's decision for them and leaves the port open to any device.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a MAC address identifies a network card. But MAC addresses are easy to copy, so one proves nothing about which device is connecting.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the owner is told, and the sign works sooner. But switching NAC off makes the exception decision for the owner and leaves the port open to anyone.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the sign fails the standard check. But a sign may never gain 802.1X; NAC designs give such devices limited access through an approved exception.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts an easily copied MAC address, and D treats NAC as a ban rather than a way to grant fitting access.
Final two: B beats C because exceptions belong to the policy owner; turning off the check first, even with a report afterward, decides for them.
Exam cue: when a device cannot meet a control, route the exception to its owner. Never bypass the control and report it afterward.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.7 (Network Access Control: health checks and limited access for remediation); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'devices that cannot use 802.1X get limited access, and exceptions go to the policy owner' (notes 4.2.8 Network Access Control (NAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. AI development environments
questions.question: A card issuer's fraud model retrains nightly on a dataset that every developer account can edit, because its AI development segment is treated as trusted. Which control should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Isolate the segment further from the office network
options.B: Scan the dataset for malware and log each nightly retraining
options.C: Limit edits to named data engineers and log every change
options.D: Encrypt the dataset so that edits cannot alter the model

questions.key_concept: Training data shapes what a model learns, so only named people should change it, and every change should be logged.
questions.pre_read: Picture one careless or hostile edit to the dataset, and follow it into tomorrow's model.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever can edit training data can quietly change what the model learns, for example teaching it to wave through one kind of fraud. So edits go only to named people who need them, and every change is logged so bad records can be traced and removed. Malware scanning is the runner-up, but poisoned records are ordinary-looking data, not malicious code, and a retraining log does not show who changed a record.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because segmenting AI work is good practice. But the risk is already inside: every developer account can edit the data, and a tighter wall does not change that.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: checking data before training is wise. But poisoned records look like normal transactions, so a malware scan passes them, and a retraining log omits who changed a record.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects data. But it stops outsiders reading files; anyone allowed to edit the dataset can still change what the model learns.

tips: Eliminate: D expects encryption to stop people who are allowed to edit, and A adds a wall around a segment whose risk is already inside it.
Final two: C beats B because poisoned records are ordinary data that malware scans pass; limiting and logging each edit prevents and traces them, which a retraining log cannot.
Exam cue: being inside an AI development segment grants no trust. Under Zero Trust, each change to training data needs a named, least-privilege identity and a log.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 2.3.2 (Targeted Poisoning); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'training data gets Zero Trust treatment, named users with least privilege and a log of every change, because tampering can poison the model' (notes 4.2.9 Segmenting AI Development Environments). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): re-angled to Zero Trust inside the AI segment (4.2.9): the stem says the segment is treated as trusted, A is a plain network-isolation distractor without a reason clause, new exam cue. Cross-domain gate (31 Oct 2026): B gains a same-form log clause so oversight wording is not on the key alone.

questions.question: A fitness app company moves its payment logic to serverless functions, and a developer says the company now has nothing left to secure. Which duty MOST clearly stays with the company?

options.A: Hardening the hypervisor on the provider's physical host servers
options.B: Patching the operating system underneath the running functions
options.C: Encrypting the provider's links between its data centers
options.D: Limiting each function's permissions and its stored secrets

questions.key_concept: Serverless hands the servers to the provider, but the customer still owns each function's code, permissions, secrets and data.
questions.pre_read: List what the company writes and configures itself when it deploys a function.
questions.correct_explanation: In serverless computing the provider runs and patches everything under the code, but the company still writes the functions and decides what each may do. Over-broad permissions or exposed secrets in a payment function are the company's risk. Patching the operating system is the runner-up because customers do that in IaaS, but with serverless the provider manages the servers and their operating systems.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because hypervisors isolate workloads. But the provider secures the hypervisor and physical hosts in every cloud service model.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: customers patch guest operating systems in IaaS. But with serverless the provider manages the servers underneath, including their operating systems.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption in transit matters. But the provider's own network between its data centers is the provider's to secure.

tips: Eliminate: A and C are the provider's own infrastructure in every service model, so they never move to the customer.
Final two: D beats B because serverless hands the servers and their operating systems to the provider; code, permissions and secrets stay with the customer.
Exam cue: however much the provider runs, the customer keeps its code, identities, permissions and data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'serverless leaves the customer owning the function's code, permissions, secrets and data' (notes 4.3.2 Virtualization and Containers in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A botanical garden keeps its plant records database in a private cloud and its public website on a public cloud, linked for exhibit data. Which deployment model should its IT coordinator record as MOST accurate?

options.A: Public cloud
options.B: Multi-cloud
options.C: Community cloud
options.D: Hybrid cloud

questions.key_concept: A hybrid cloud joins two or more deployment models, such as private and public; using several providers is called multi-cloud.
questions.pre_read: List where each of the garden's systems runs and how the two are linked.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST defines a hybrid cloud as two or more distinct cloud infrastructures, such as private and public, bound together so data and applications can move between them. The garden joins a private cloud to a public one, so it is hybrid, and the link between them needs securing. Multi-cloud is the runner-up because two clouds are involved, but the term means using several providers, which may all be public.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the website runs on a public cloud. But the records database sits in a private cloud, so the whole setup is not public.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: two clouds are in use. But multi-cloud means using several providers; joining a private cloud to a public one is a hybrid of two models.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the setup links clouds together. But a community cloud is built for several organizations with shared needs, not for one garden.

tips: Eliminate: C needs several organizations with shared needs, and A would fit only if every part ran on a public cloud.
Final two: D beats B because the setup mixes two deployment models; multi-cloud is about using several providers.
Exam cue: hybrid mixes models (private plus public); multi-cloud mixes providers. Count models first, then providers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: deployment models)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a hybrid cloud joins two or more models, and the links between them must be secured' (notes 4.3.4 Cloud Deployment Models). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4.3 Cloud security. Cloud roles and agreements
questions.question: An e-sports league's cloud contract promises 99.95% uptime, and its manager says the league therefore needs no plan for provider outages. Which reply from the IT coordinator is MOST accurate?

options.A: That target still allows about four hours of outage a year
options.B: Service credits in the contract will make up for any outage
options.C: The provider's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covers outage planning
options.D: The provider's backups stop outages from affecting the league

questions.key_concept: A service level agreement sets an availability target and a remedy such as service credits; outages still happen, so continuity plans must cover them.
questions.pre_read: Picture the league's biggest match night falling inside an outage.
questions.correct_explanation: An uptime figure is a target, not a promise of no outages: NIST notes that 99.95% still means about 4.4 hours of downtime a year, and scheduled maintenance is often excluded. Availability must be covered in continuity planning. Service credits are the runner-up because the contract does offer a remedy, but credits usually refund part of the fee, not the league's lost matches or income.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: service level agreements do offer credits when targets are missed. But credits usually refund part of the fee; they do not restore lost matches or income.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a certificate shows strong provider controls. But it covers the provider's own scope, not the league's plans for when a service is down.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because backups protect the league's data. But backups restore data after a loss; they do not keep the service running while the provider is down.

tips: Eliminate: D confuses backups, which restore data, with keeping the service running, and C stretches a provider's certificate over the customer's own planning.
Final two: A beats B because an agreement's remedy is usually a partial refund; the outage still happens, so the league must plan for it.
Exam cue: a service level agreement sets a target and a remedy, not a guarantee. Keep continuity plans for the hours it still allows.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.8 (Availability: 99.95% availability still means about 4.38 hours of downtime a year)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'the service level agreement sets a target, such as 99.9% availability, and a remedy; outages still happen' (notes 4.3.6 Cloud Roles and Agreements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): D was the mirror of the key ('a few seconds' against 'about four hours'); it is now the backups-equal-availability misconception, so no opposite pair points to the key.

questions.question: After moving its case files, a legal-aid charity is leaving a cloud service that stored them encrypted under keys the charity manages. What should its system administrator do to BEST make every remaining copy unreadable?

options.A: Re-encrypt the files under new keys before deleting them
options.B: Destroy the encryption keys that protect the files
options.C: Delete every case file and its old encrypted versions
options.D: Cancel the subscription so the provider erases the disks

questions.key_concept: Customers cannot wipe a cloud provider's disks; destroying the encryption keys they control makes every remaining copy unreadable.
questions.pre_read: Think about where copies of a cloud file live besides the folder you can see.
questions.correct_explanation: Cloud data sits in replicas and backups the charity cannot reach, and it cannot wipe the provider's disks. Because the files are encrypted with keys the charity controls, destroying those keys makes every copy unreadable; NIST notes that this cryptographic erase may be the only workable purge for cloud storage. Deleting the files is the runner-up because it clears what the charity sees, but replicas and backups remain.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fresh keys feel safer. But older replicas and backups stay encrypted under the old keys, which still exist and can still decrypt them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: deleting files and old versions removes the copies the charity can see. But replicas and provider backups can stay readable for some time.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because providers do remove data after an account closes. But the timing and method are the provider's, and the charity cannot verify them.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves the old keys able to read older copies, and D leaves the job to the provider's own timing.
Final two: B beats C because deleting leaves replicas and backups behind; destroying the keys makes every copy unreadable at once.
Exam cue: for data you cannot physically reach, destroying the keys you control is how you make every copy unreadable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 3.1.2 (Purge Sanitization Method: for cloud storage, cryptographic erase may be the only viable purge technique); NIST SP 800-144 Section 4.7 (Data Protection)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'at exit, customers cannot wipe the provider's disks, so they delete data and destroy its keys' (notes 4.3.7 Protecting Data in the Cloud). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): the stem now says the files were moved first, so destroying the keys loses nothing the charity must keep, and uses the canonical role 'system administrator'; B no longer echoes the stem's 'stored'.

questions.question: A parking garage operator's switches answer SNMPv2c monitoring queries using the community string 'public', and the network lead approves all switch changes. What should the junior network technician do FIRST?

options.A: Move SNMP to an unusual port so scanners miss it
options.B: Change the community string from 'public' to 'private'
options.C: Ask the network lead to approve moving the switches to SNMPv3
options.D: Move every switch to SNMPv3 tonight, then tell the network lead

questions.key_concept: SNMP versions 1 and 2c send community strings in cleartext; SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption. Device changes go through whoever approves them.
questions.pre_read: Picture what an eavesdropper on the network sees during each monitoring query.
questions.correct_explanation: SNMPv2c sends its community string, in effect a password, in cleartext, and 'public' is a well-known default, so SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption is the right fix. The network lead approves switch changes, so the technician asks the lead to approve the move to SNMPv3. Changing every switch tonight is the runner-up because it applies the right fix, but doing it without approval bypasses change control and risks breaking monitoring.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because an odd port looks hidden. But scanners find services on any port, and the community string still crosses the network in cleartext.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it removes the default value. But 'private' is another well-known default, and SNMPv2c still sends it in cleartext.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: SNMPv3 is the right protocol. But the network lead approves switch changes, and an unapproved change across every switch could break monitoring or the network.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on an unusual port, and B swaps one well-known, cleartext community string for another.
Final two: C beats D because the network lead approves switch changes; even the right fix goes through the person who approves it.
Exam cue: pick the encrypted version of the protocol (SNMPv3, SSH, SFTP), then route the change through whoever approves it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-8(1) (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'choose the encrypted protocol for the same job, and report cleartext protocols to the owner' (notes 4.1.5 Ports, Protocols and Secure Alternatives). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): key C reworded from Report to Ask (bank-wide Report/Ask tell); meaning unchanged.

questions.question: A coworking space's firewall applies the first matching rule: rule 1 allows internet use, and rule 2 blocks a banned file-sharing site, yet members reach it. Which change should the network technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Move the block rule to the top, above the allow rule
options.B: Repeat the block rule at the bottom of the list
options.C: Delete the allow rule so the block can take effect
options.D: Block the site in each member's browser settings

questions.key_concept: Where a firewall applies the first matching rule, a broad rule placed above a narrower one hides it, so specific rules go first.
questions.pre_read: Walk one request to the banned site down the rule list from the top.
questions.correct_explanation: This firewall stops at the first rule that matches. A request to the banned site matches rule 1, the broad allow, so rule 2 is never read. Placing the narrow block above it stops the site while all other internet use still matches rule 1. Deleting rule 1 is the runner-up because the site would then be blocked, but so would every other site members need.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it adds the block again. But a rule at the bottom still sits below rule 1, which matches the traffic first.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: removing rule 1 would stop the site. But it also cuts members off from the rest of the internet they rely on.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because browsers can block sites. But members' own devices are outside the space's control and settings are easy to change; the firewall is where the policy is enforced.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the block below the rule that matches first, and D moves enforcement to members' own browsers, which the space cannot control.
Final two: A beats C because reordering keeps internet access for everything else; deleting the allow rule cuts members off entirely.
Exam cue: where the first match wins, put specific rules above broad ones, and fix the order with the narrowest change.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 5.2.2 (Policy Configuration: many firewalls check rules in order until a match is found)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'rules are read from the top and the first match wins, so specific rules go first' (notes 4.1.7 Firewalls: Ports and Applications). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): A and C reworded (same actions; 'allow rule' now appears in both) so the domain's longest-key rate stays inside the 15-30% band.

questions.subtopic: 4.1 Network security. AI in traffic monitoring
questions.question: A sailing school's AI monitor flags the finance director's laptop calling a new domain each minute over encrypted traffic, like malware checking in; verification is the analyst's runbook task. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the finance director if the laptop's connections are expected
options.B: Close the alert, as the monitor cannot read encrypted traffic
options.C: Let the monitor block the laptop, then close the alert
options.D: Review the connections in the laptop's logs and flow records

questions.key_concept: AI monitors read timing, volume and destination even in encrypted traffic; when the runbook assigns you an alert, verify it yourself first.
questions.pre_read: Picture the possible explanations for these connections, harmless and harmful.
questions.correct_explanation: Encryption hides content, not timing, volume or destination, and a steady beat to a brand-new domain is typical of malware. The runbook gives verification to the on-shift analyst, so they check the connections against the laptop's logs and flow records and escalate if the alert holds up. Asking the finance director is the runner-up because they use the laptop, but the runbook assigns the check, and asking first could alert whoever is behind the connections.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the director may know of a legitimate app. But the runbook assigns verification to the analyst, and asking first could alert an insider or attacker.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption hides the content. But AI monitors judge timing, volume and destination, which encryption does not hide.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because automatic blocking is fast. But AI scores can be wrong, and blocking a director's laptop is a high-impact step that needs a person's check.

tips: Eliminate: B forgets that timing, volume and destination stay visible under encryption, and C hands a high-impact block to the AI tool unchecked.
Final two: D beats A because the runbook assigns verification to the analyst; a named laptop owner does not take over a task the procedure gives you.
Exam cue: treat an AI alert as a lead to verify. If the runbook gives you the check, do it before routing the case elsewhere.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-4(13) (System Monitoring | Analyze Traffic and Event Patterns); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IR-4 (Incident Handling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI models still analyze timing, volume and destinations when traffic is encrypted; treat AI detection as an assistant whose alerts are verified' (notes 4.1.9 AI in Traffic Monitoring, IDS and Firewalls). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. questions.question: A pet-supplies web shop's security analyst finds attackers hiding commands in the text fields of its order form. At which OSI layer should the analyst's proposed filter work to BEST catch them?

options.A: Layer 6, the presentation layer
options.B: Layer 2, the data link layer
options.C: Layer 7, the application layer
options.D: Layer 3, the network layer

questions.key_concept: A control works only at its own layer; spotting harmful content inside web requests needs a layer 7 control, such as an application-aware firewall.
questions.pre_read: Think about which layer actually reads what a customer types into a form.
questions.correct_explanation: The commands hide in what customers type into the form, which is application data that only layer 7, the application layer, interprets. An application-aware firewall or web filter working there can read form fields and block harmful input. The presentation layer is the runner-up because it handles how data is formatted, encoded or encrypted, but it does not judge what form input means to the web application.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: layer 6 handles data formats, encoding and encryption, so typed text seems to fit. But whether form input hides a command is the application's business, at layer 7.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because switches can filter frames. But layer 2 handles local delivery by hardware address and never reads form fields.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because routers and packet filters work here. But they read IP addresses, not the content of a web request.

tips: Eliminate: B delivers frames by hardware address, and D routes packets by IP address; neither reads what a customer types.
Final two: C beats A because the attack lives in what the form input means to the application; the presentation layer only formats, encodes or encrypts data.
Exam cue: name the layer where the attack lives, then pick a control that works at that layer.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 2.1.3 (Application Firewalls); NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1 Section 2.1 (The Need for Network Layer Security: controls at each layer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a control protects only its own layer; a switch setting cannot stop an attack inside a web request' (notes 4.1.2 The OSI Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An online toy store's security team is installing its first inline intrusion prevention system (IPS) before the holiday rush. Which starting setup should the junior analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Install it in place of the store's firewall
options.B: Run it alert-only, logging what it would block
options.C: Turn on blocking for the vendor's recommended rule set
options.D: Rely on its automatic blocking, with no alert review

questions.key_concept: A new IPS starts in an alert-only (simulation) mode so its rules can be tuned before blocking, which avoids stopping legitimate business traffic.
questions.pre_read: Picture the busiest shopping day with the new system sitting in the traffic path.
questions.correct_explanation: A new IPS raises many false positives until it is tuned, and because it sits inline, every wrong block stops real orders. Alert-only mode, which NIST calls simulation mode, logs what it would block so the team can tune first. The vendor's recommended rules are the runner-up because they are a sensible start, but until they are tuned to the store's traffic they could turn away real shoppers in the busiest season.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because both sit in the traffic path. But a firewall decides which traffic is allowed at all; an IPS only hunts for attacks inside allowed traffic.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the vendor's recommended rules are a sensible start. But they are not tuned to this store's traffic, and an inline device stops whatever it blocks, real orders included.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because prevention is automatic. But alerts still need triage, and an unwatched IPS lets wrong blocks and missed attacks go unnoticed.

tips: Eliminate: A removes the firewall, whose allow-and-deny job an IPS does not take over, and D assumes automatic prevention needs no one watching.
Final two: B beats C because even recommended rules need tuning to the store's own traffic; blocking before tuning stops real business traffic.
Exam cue: new blocking controls start in watch mode. Tune them on real traffic, then switch on blocking.

questions.question: At an insurance call center, a wireless scan finds an access point plugged into a meeting-room wall jack; an employee installed it for better signal. Which risk should the network technician report as GREATEST?

options.A: Outsiders could use it to reach the wired network directly
options.B: Its radio could interfere with the official Wi-Fi channels
options.C: Staff using it could bypass the company's web filtering
options.D: It could reveal the hidden name of the official Wi-Fi network

questions.key_concept: An unapproved access point on the wired network gives anyone in radio range a way in that goes around perimeter controls.
questions.pre_read: Picture someone in the parking lot with a laptop, and trace where the new access point lets them go.
questions.correct_explanation: An access point plugged into the wired network extends it to anyone in radio range, and an employee's device is unlikely to have the company's encryption, sign-in or monitoring. NIST notes that a rogue access point can give a backdoor into the wired network that bypasses firewalls. Interference is the runner-up because an extra radio can disrupt the official Wi-Fi, but that slows service rather than exposing internal systems.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an extra radio can crowd the official channels. But that only slows the Wi-Fi; the greater risk is outsiders reaching internal systems through the device.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the device is unmanaged. But on a company wall jack, its traffic usually crosses the company's filters, and a filtering gap matters less than outsiders reaching internal systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because extra radios add exposure. But hidden network names are easy to find anyway; hiding one was never real protection.

tips: Eliminate: C overlooks that traffic through the device usually still crosses the company's network and filters, and D treats a hidden network name as protection worth losing.
Final two: A beats B because a backdoor into the wired network exposes internal systems; interference only slows the Wi-Fi.
Exam cue: any unapproved device that bridges radio to the wired network is a door around the perimeter. Rate access above inconvenience.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-153 Section 3.1.1 (Attack Monitoring: a rogue access point can give a backdoor into the wired network, bypassing firewalls)

Audit fix-up (31 Oct 2026): C (Bluetooth pairing) was a strawman; it is now the real misconception that an unmanaged access point bypasses web filtering.

questions.question: A youth sports league must install its own approved monitoring agent on the operating system of every server behind its registration app. Which cloud service model MOST directly lets its volunteer system administrator do this?

options.A: Software as a service (SaaS)
options.B: Platform as a service (PaaS)
options.C: Function as a service (FaaS, serverless)
options.D: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)

questions.key_concept: Only IaaS hands the customer the guest operating system, so software that must run on that operating system needs IaaS.
questions.pre_read: Sort the layers under the app into those the league needs to touch and those it does not.
questions.correct_explanation: Only infrastructure as a service hands the customer the guest operating system, so only IaaS lets the league install its own agent there; the league then also patches and hardens those systems. Platform as a service is the runner-up because the league still deploys its own app, but the provider runs the operating system beneath it and customers cannot install software there.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it needs the least work. But in SaaS the provider runs the whole application stack, and customers never reach its servers.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the league still deploys and secures its own app in PaaS. But the provider runs the operating system underneath, so the league cannot install an agent on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it also runs the league's own code. But function as a service (serverless) hides the servers entirely; there is no operating system the customer can reach.

tips: Eliminate: A and C give the customer no operating system to manage; the provider runs every server in both.
Final two: D beats B because only IaaS gives the customer the guest operating system; in PaaS the provider runs it.
Exam cue: if a task needs software installed on the server's own operating system, look for IaaS; PaaS and serverless keep that layer with the provider.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models)

Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D4 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): C now uses its acronym like the other options.

questions.question: A dance school's own booking app runs on platform as a service (PaaS), and its email is software as a service (SaaS). Which split for fixing a code flaw in each is MOST accurate?

options.A: The school fixes the flaws in both applications
options.B: Each provider fixes the flaw in the application it hosts
options.C: The school fixes the booking app; the email provider fixes email
options.D: The school fixes the email; the platform provider fixes the booking app

questions.key_concept: In SaaS the provider runs and fixes the application itself; in PaaS the provider runs only the platform, so the customer fixes its own application.
questions.pre_read: Take each service on its own, and ask what the school controls in it.
questions.correct_explanation: Shared responsibility is not the same in every model. In PaaS the provider runs the operating system and runtime, but the booking app is the school's own code, so the school fixes it. In SaaS the provider runs the whole application, so it fixes the email flaw. The school fixing both is the runner-up because it does fix its own app and set its email options, but it cannot reach the SaaS provider's code.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the school does fix its own booking app and sets its email settings. But in SaaS the provider runs the application, so only it can fix the code.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a PaaS provider patches a lot. But it patches the operating system and runtime beneath the app; the booking app is the school's own code to fix.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it splits the work. But it reverses the split: a platform provider does not fix customers' code, and the school cannot reach the email provider's code.

tips: Eliminate: B has the platform provider fixing the school's own code, and D reverses which party fixes each application.
Final two: C beats A because in SaaS the provider runs the application and its code; the school sets the email options but cannot fix its code.
Exam cue: never apply one split to every cloud service. Check the model first, then ask who controls the layer with the flaw.

questions.question: A recycling company's tuned AI model sits on a cloud endpoint, and a review shows the endpoint answers anyone on the internet without signing in. Which fix should the security analyst propose FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the provider's encryption of the stored model files
options.B: Allow only authenticated, approved callers to reach it
options.C: Retrain the model to refuse questions from unknown users
options.D: Ask the AI provider to restrict who can reach the endpoint

questions.key_concept: On a cloud AI platform, who can reach a customer's model is the customer's setting, and access control comes from authentication, not model behavior.
questions.pre_read: Picture a stranger who finds the endpoint's address tomorrow.
questions.correct_explanation: The provider secures the AI platform, but who can call a customer's deployed model is a customer setting, like any other cloud access control. The fix is to require authentication and allow only approved apps or users. Asking the provider is the runner-up because the endpoint runs on its platform, but access settings for the company's own model are the company's to change.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects stored files. But it does nothing to stop anyone calling the running model through its open endpoint.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models can be trained to refuse requests. But that is behavior, not access control; strangers can still reach the model and try to trick it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the endpoint does run on the provider's platform. But who may call the company's own model is a setting the company controls, not the provider.

tips: Eliminate: C expects model training to replace access control, and A confuses encryption at rest with controlling who can call the model.
Final two: B beats D because access to the customer's own model is a customer setting; the provider secures only the platform beneath it.
Exam cue: on a cloud AI service, the provider secures the platform; data, models, access and settings stay with the customer.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement); NIST SP 800-145 Section 2 (The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing: service models)

questions.subtopic: 4.2 Network security architecture. Zero Trust principles
questions.question: At a bicycle maker adopting Zero Trust, an engineer passes multifactor sign-in at 9 a.m., and at noon their laptop's malware protection is switched off. What should MOST appropriately happen to the engineer's access?

options.A: It is rechecked and limited until the laptop is healthy again
options.B: It stays open, since the laptop is on the office network
options.C: It is cut off, and the engineer's account is disabled
options.D: It is rechecked, and the morning's sign-in still covers it

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust keeps checking: access is granted per session and evaluated again when identity, device health or context change.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the morning's checks proved, and what has changed since.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero Trust does not verify once and trust for the day. Access decisions use identity, device health and context, and are made again as conditions change, so a laptop that loses its malware protection has its access rechecked and limited until it is healthy. Disabling the engineer's account is the runner-up because it removes the risk, but the identity is still valid; the device is the problem.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the laptop sits inside the office. But Zero Trust grants nothing for network location; each request is judged on identity and health.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it removes the risk at once. But the engineer's identity is still valid; the device changed, so Zero Trust limits access until it is healthy.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because multifactor sign-in is strong. But it proves who the user is, not whether their laptop is healthy, so a fair recheck must flag the laptop.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the office network location, and D treats the morning's proof of identity as proof of device health.
Final two: A beats C because the change is in the device, not the identity; Zero Trust limits access until the laptop is healthy instead of disabling a valid account.
Exam cue: never trust, always verify, and verify again when something changes: identity, device health or context.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-207 Section 2.1 (Tenets of Zero Trust)
